items.title: Egyptian Coffins Reveal Shocking Ancient Practice
items.description:
NEW ARCHAEOLOGY!  
 
Archaeologist Giselle Kiraly comes face to face with ancient Egyptian coffins, including one which may have been re-used for multiple corpses. Join us as we learn how these coffins were built, what the decorations mean and how they're being preserved and analysed in the Petrie Museum.

0:00 Intro
0:39 Ptolemaic coffin 
5:34 Late Period coffin - Religious beliefs 
8:42 Third Intermediate Period coffin - Artwork and personalisation
13:59 Third Intermediate Period coffin - Wood
items.why_watch: Archaeologist Giselle Kiraly walks through actual Egyptian coffins at the Petrie Museum, including one that appears to have been reused for multiple bodies — a detail that quietly reframes assumptions about ancient burial as a fixed, sacred ritual. At nearly 29 minutes, it earns its runtime by grounding abstract Egyptology in close physical observation of real objects.

discovery_articles.title: 14 Mesmerizing Mazes and Labyrinths
discovery_articles.snippet: Since antiquity, mazes and labyrinths have been places of spiritual reflection and deep contemplation. The famous Egyptian Labyrinth at Hawara was built around 1860 BCE during the reign of Pharaoh Amenemhat III, though 2D depictions of the classic seven-circuit design appear as early as 2000 BCE in clay tablets from the Mediterranean. Mazes, too, have origins in ancient Egypt, primarily serving to keep looters away from the tombs of the important and wealthy.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Before mazes were garden party novelties, they were deadly serious architecture — the Egyptian labyrinth at Hawara was essentially a 4,000-year-old security system for the dead. The oldest known labyrinth design, scratched into a clay tablet around 2000 BCE, predates the Minotaur myth by centuries, which means the symbol arrived long before the story caught up.

discovery_articles.snippet: The colorful nasturtiums at the artist's house and gardens have been hit particularly hard this summer as France grapples with a record 52 heatwave days
discovery_articles.ferns_note: There's something quietly devastating about the flowers Monet painted obsessively — his living color palette — now wilting under the very climate his era helped set in motion. The garden at Giverny isn't just a tourist site; it's a living artwork slowly being undone by time and heat.

It's the most unexpected monument to resilience you'll find behind glass.

discovery_articles.snippet: Animal skeletons, Neolithic tools and pop culture memorabilia are among the dozens of objects to be displayed in the reopened “Nature and Us” exhibition
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A gallery sealed off during the Blitz and left untouched for nearly 80 years sounds like the opening of a gothic novel — but the Natural History Museum's reopened wing is the real thing, a time capsule of Neolithic tools and animal bones finally breathing public air again. Whatever was quietly gathering dust in there, it waited patiently.
